subject: Cognitive Science
title: Eye Movements in Reading
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Eye Movements in Reading.

hook.text: Your eyes don't glide smoothly across text. They hop in jumps called saccades, landing roughly every 7 letters.

buildup.text: During each fixation, you only see about 15 letters clearly. The rest is blurry peripheral vision.

discovery.text: Common words get shorter fixations. Rare or surprising words hold the eye longer—the brain needs more time.

twist.text: About 10–15% of saccades go backward. These regressions spike at confusing passages—the eyes diagnose the problem.

climax.text: Eye-tracking lets researchers see comprehension in real time—every pause and backtrack maps a moment of thought.

punchline.text: Your eyes reveal what your mind is struggling with.

quiz.question: What is a saccade?
options: A rapid eye jump during reading

details.summary: Reading is not a smooth sweep across the page. Eyes make rapid jumps called saccades, landing on fixation points for 200 to 250 milliseconds each. Short function words are often skipped; long and rare words receive longer fixations.
details.whyItMatters: Eye-tracking has become the primary tool for studying reading. Fixation patterns reveal moment-by-moment mental processing that self-reports cannot capture.
takeaways: Eyes jump between fixation points rather than gliding smoothly
Fixation duration reflects processing difficulty of a word
Rare and long words receive longer fixation times

faq.question: What is a saccade exactly?
faq.answer: A saccade is a rapid ballistic eye movement lasting 20 to 40 milliseconds that repositions the fovea. During saccades, vision is suppressed, so information is extracted only during fixations.

faq.question: Why do readers sometimes look backward in a text?
faq.answer: Backward eye movements, called regressions, occur when comprehension breaks down. A garden path sentence triggers regressions to reparse. Regressions account for about 10 to 15 percent of eye movements in normal reading and increase with text difficulty, ambiguity, and reader fatigue.
